sections.title: Storage, data transfer and organization billing

topics.title: How AWS charges: the three pricing principles

kcs.statement: AWS's three fundamental cost drivers are compute, storage and outbound data transfer; inbound data transfer from the internet is generally free.
AWS pricing follows three principles: pay as you go for what you use, save when you commit to a term, and pay less per unit as your usage volume grows.

The AWS Free Tier includes always-free offers that never expire (such as Lambda's 1 million free requests per month) alongside time-limited offers for new accounts; usage above the free limits is billed at normal rates.

serves.reason: Estimating any workload's cost starts from knowing which dimensions (compute, storage, data out) AWS bills on.

problem_ideas: A startup's first bill shows charges for EC2, S3 and 'DataTransfer-Out-Bytes'; which line is the one that is usually free in the other direction?

topics.title: On-Demand pricing and Reserved Instances

kcs.statement: On-Demand Instances are billed per second (60-second minimum for Linux) or per hour with no long-term commitment, which suits short-term, spiky or unpredictable workloads that must not be interrupted.
Reserved Instances commit to a 1- or 3-year term for up to 72% off On-Demand; All Upfront gives the largest discount, then Partial Upfront, then No Upfront, and a 3-year term beats a 1-year term.

A Standard RI gives the larger discount but cannot change instance family; a Convertible RI can be exchanged for a different instance family, operating system or tenancy in return for a smaller discount.

A Regional RI applies its discount to matching usage in any Availability Zone of its Region and, for Linux, across sizes within the same instance family; a zonal RI also reserves capacity in one specific AZ.

serves.reason: Choosing between On-Demand and Reserved Instances and estimating the saving is the core of the o5 workload decision.

problem_ideas: An m5.large costs $0.096/hour On-Demand and $0.060/hour as a 1-year RI: predict the yearly saving for one always-on instance.

topics.title: Savings Plans: Compute vs EC2 Instance

kcs.statement: A Savings Plan commits to a fixed spend in dollars per hour for 1 or 3 years; usage up to the commitment gets the discounted rate and usage above it is billed at On-Demand rates.
Compute Savings Plans (up to 66% off) apply automatically across EC2 instance families, sizes, Regions and operating systems, and also to Fargate and Lambda usage.
EC2 Instance Savings Plans (up to 72% off) lock the discount to one instance family in one Region, trading flexibility for a deeper saving similar to a Standard RI.

serves.reason: o5 names Savings Plans as one of the four options the learner must choose between and justify.

requires.reason: Savings Plans are defined as a discount off On-Demand rates and contrasted with RI commitments.

topics.title: Spot Instances: deep discounts, interruptible

kcs.statement: Spot Instances use spare EC2 capacity for up to 90% off On-Demand, but AWS can reclaim them with a two-minute interruption notice.
Spot suits fault-tolerant, flexible, stateless work such as batch jobs, CI builds, big-data processing and rendering, and is the wrong choice for databases or anything that cannot be interrupted.

serves.reason: Spot is one of the four purchasing options o5 requires the learner to choose and justify.

requires.reason: The Spot discount and its trade-off are stated relative to On-Demand pricing.

topics.title: Dedicated Hosts, Dedicated Instances, reservations

kcs.statement: A Dedicated Host is a whole physical server for your use with visibility of its sockets and cores, chosen to bring per-socket or per-core software licenses (BYOL) or meet strict compliance rules; it is the most expensive EC2 option.
Dedicated Instances run on hardware dedicated to one AWS account but give no visibility or control over the physical host, so they cannot satisfy server-bound licensing.

On-Demand Capacity Reservations guarantee EC2 capacity in a specific Availability Zone for any duration and are billed at On-Demand rates whether used or not; they give no discount unless combined with Savings Plans or Regional RIs.

serves.reason: BYOL and compliance questions that hinge on Dedicated Hosts are a recurring CLF-C02 item outside the four options in o5.

topics.title: Choosing an EC2 purchasing option

kcs.statement: A steady 24/7 workload expected to run for a year or more belongs on Reserved Instances or Savings Plans, while a short-lived or unpredictable workload belongs on On-Demand.
A common cost-optimal fleet covers the steady baseline with Savings Plans or RIs, the peaks with On-Demand, and interruptible extra work with Spot.
Relative saving = 1 − (discounted hourly rate ÷ On-Demand hourly rate); for example $0.06 versus $0.10 an hour is a 40% saving, about $350 a year for one instance running all 8,760 hours.

topics.title: Storage pricing: S3 classes, EBS and EFS

kcs.statement: S3 cost has four parts: gigabyte-months stored (priced by storage class), requests, data retrieval for infrequent-access and Glacier classes, and data transferred out.

Infrequent-access and Glacier classes cost less to store but charge per-GB retrieval fees and have minimum storage durations: 30 days for Standard-IA, 90 days for Glacier Flexible Retrieval and 180 days for Glacier Deep Archive.
EBS bills for the gigabytes you provision whether or not you fill them, while EFS and S3 bill only for the gigabytes actually stored.

serves.reason: The exam guide's Task 4.1 explicitly lists pricing for storage options and tiers.

topics.title: Data transfer costs: in, out, across AZs and Regions

kcs.statement: Data transfer into AWS from the internet is free, while data transferred out to the internet is charged per GB, with the per-GB rate falling at higher monthly volumes.
Traffic between Availability Zones and between Regions is charged per GB, while traffic within one AZ over private IP addresses is free, so multi-AZ and cross-Region designs add transfer cost.
Data transfer from AWS origins such as S3 or EC2 to CloudFront is free, so serving content through CloudFront can lower data-out costs compared with serving directly from the origin.

serves.reason: Data transfer pricing is a recurring cost-trap question on the exam.

problem_ideas: Rank by cost per GB: internet to EC2, EC2 to EC2 in the same AZ via private IP, EC2 across AZs, EC2 to another Region.

topics.title: Consolidated billing in AWS Organizations

kcs.statement: Consolidated billing in AWS Organizations gives the management account one bill for all member accounts at no extra charge, while still itemizing each account's charges.
Consolidated billing combines usage across accounts for tiered pricing, so ten accounts storing 10 TB each in S3 are priced as 100 TB and reach cheaper tiers sooner.

Reserved Instance and Savings Plans discounts are shared across all accounts in the organization by default, so an unused RI in one account can discount matching usage in another; the management account can turn sharing off.

topics.title: Cost allocation tags: splitting the bill

kcs.statement: Cost allocation tags are key-value tags that must be activated in the Billing and Cost Management console before they appear as a dimension in cost reports; activation normally affects subsequent reporting, but management-account users can request up to 12 months of backfill for periods when the resource already carried the tag.

There are two kinds of cost allocation tags, AWS-generated tags (such as aws:createdBy) and user-defined tags (such as Project=checkout), and they are used to split one bill by team, project or environment.

topics.title: AWS Budgets: alerts before you overspend

kcs.statement: AWS Budgets tracks custom cost budgets, usage budgets, and Reserved Instance or Savings Plans utilization and coverage budgets against thresholds you set.
AWS Budgets sends alerts by email or SNS when actual or forecasted spend crosses a threshold, unlike a CloudWatch billing alarm, which fires only on actual estimated charges.
Budget actions can respond automatically to a breached budget by applying an IAM policy or SCP, or by stopping specific EC2 or RDS instances.

topics.title: Cost Explorer vs the Cost and Usage Report

kcs.statement: Cost Explorer visualizes historical spend and usage in charts filterable by service, account, Region or tag, and forecasts future spend from past usage.
Cost Explorer also provides Reserved Instance and Savings Plans purchase recommendations and reports on their utilization and coverage.
The Cost and Usage Report is AWS's most detailed billing data, with hourly line items including resource IDs and tags, delivered to an S3 bucket for analysis with Athena, QuickSight or Redshift.

topics.title: Compute Optimizer: rightsizing recommendations

kcs.statement: AWS Compute Optimizer uses machine learning on CloudWatch utilization metrics to recommend right-sized EC2 instances, Auto Scaling groups, EBS volumes, Lambda memory settings and ECS services on Fargate.

Compute Optimizer focuses on resources that are over- or under-provisioned, while Trusted Advisor runs broad checks across cost, security, fault tolerance, performance, service limits and operational excellence.

topics.title: Choosing a cost management tool

kcs.statement: Pick the cost tool by the question asked: the future cost of an unbuilt design → Pricing Calculator; an alert before overspending → AWS Budgets; what was spent and why → Cost Explorer.
When finance needs hourly, resource-level billing data in its own BI or SQL tools, the answer is the Cost and Usage Report rather than Cost Explorer.
To find waste, use Compute Optimizer for rightsizing over-provisioned compute and Trusted Advisor's cost optimization checks for idle resources such as unattached EBS volumes or idle load balancers.

topics.title: AWS Support plans today: Basic to Unified Operations

kcs.statement: Basic Support is free for every account and includes 24/7 account and billing customer service, documentation, re:Post, the Health Dashboard and core Trusted Advisor checks, but no technical support cases.

Business Support+ is the entry paid plan in AWS's current Support lineup, giving 24/7 technical support and a response target of under 30 minutes for critical cases such as a business-critical system being down.
Enterprise Support targets a response in under 15 minutes when a business-critical system is down and includes a designated technical account manager.
Unified Operations is the top Support tier for mission-critical workloads, targeting a response within 5 minutes on critical incidents from an Incident Management Engineer.

serves.reason: o5 requires choosing the cheapest Support plan that meets a stated response-time need, which needs the current plan ladder. (The finding's request to also update clf-trusted-advisor targets an earlier stage's topic and cannot be changed in this stage pass.)

topics.title: Legacy plans: Developer, Business, Enterprise On-Ramp

kcs.statement: Legacy Developer Support gives business-hours email access to technical support, with responses in under 24 business hours for general guidance and under 12 business hours for an impaired system, suited to testing and early development.

Legacy Business Support gives 24/7 phone, chat and email technical support and all Trusted Advisor checks, with responses in under 4 hours for an impaired production system and under 1 hour for a production system that is down.
Legacy Enterprise On-Ramp targets under 30 minutes for a business-critical system down and gives access to a pool of technical account managers rather than a designated one.

serves.reason: Developer, Business and Enterprise On-Ramp are being retired in favour of the current plans, but CLF-C02 items written before the change can still name them, so recognising their response targets protects exam marks.

AWS Professional Services is AWS's own paid team of experts that works alongside customers and partners on large outcomes such as data-center migrations.
